citation.title: Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?

standing_assumptions:
The work is Aronow and Samii, ‘Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?’, American Journal of Political Science 60(1): 250–267 (2016). Printed p. 249 + N is PDF p. N; Appendices A, B and C are printed pp. 262–265 (PDF pp. 13–16). Every passage below was read from the page images. The official erratum (AJPS 61(2): 504, 2017) concerns printed pp. 258 and 260 only and touches no target.

[Sampling and data: section ‘Data, Potential Outcomes, and Causal Effects’, p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “Suppose that we begin with a population of interest and draw a sample indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, n$. We assume that the sample is self-weighting and representative—each member of the population has an equal probability of being selected. … All of the results in this article continue to apply if we substitute sampling from a fixed population with the super-population assumption. For all $i$ that appear in the sample, we measure (a) a causal factor of interest, or “treatment,” $D_i$, which may be continuous or binary; (b) a $K$-length row vector of control variables, $X_i$, that exhibit no perfect colinearities or measurement error; and (c) an outcome, $Y_i$. The sampling or super-population assumption implies that $D_i$, $X_i$, and $Y_i$ are random variables, although not necessarily independent.”

[Potential outcomes: p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “for every potential value of $D_i$, each unit $i$ is assumed to possess a well-defined response. Thus, if $D_i$ can take on the values $d_1, d_2, \ldots$, then unit $i$’s potential outcomes are given by the corresponding values $Y_i(d_1), Y_i(d_2), \ldots$.”

[Expression (1): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we suppose that potential outcomes take the following form: $Y_i(d) = Y_i(0) + \tau_i \cdot d$, (1) where $\tau_i$ is the causal effect for unit $i$ and $d$ is an arbitrary value of $D_i$. When the treatment is binary, $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$, then this characterization is completely general.”

[Expression (2): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we assume that the control variables in $X_i$ are indeed sufficient for removing any confounding in the relationship between $D_i$ on $Y_i$, so that $(Y_i(0), \tau_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i | X_i$. (2)”

[Expression (3): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “We also assume that the conditional expected value of $D_i$ can be represented as a linear combination of the covariates in $X_i$. … Formally, this assumption may be written as $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$, (3) where $V_i = (1 \quad X_i)$, $\omega$ is a $K + 1$ column vector of coefficients, and $\mathrm{E}[.]$ averages over the units in the population.”

[Expression (4): p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “The goal is to estimate the average causal effect for the population. This is simply the expected value of the unit-level causal effects: $\bar\tau = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}\right]$, (4) where $d' \neq d$ are two arbitrary values that are possible for $D_i$.”

[Regression: section ‘Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$Y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + X_i\gamma + \epsilon_i$, (6) where $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are model coefficients and $\epsilon_i$ is an error term. … We fit Model (6) using OLS to obtain estimates of the parameters, $\hat\alpha$, $\hat\beta$, and $\hat\gamma$. The estimate $\hat\beta$ is our regression estimate of the causal effect of $D_i$.”

[Expression (7) and the weight: p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$. (7) We call $w_i$ the multiple regression weight for unit $i$. The relation $\overset{p}{\to}$ refers to convergence in probability as the sample size, $n$, gets larger and larger”.

[Effective sample and estimated weights: section ‘The Effective Sample from Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 255 (PDF p. 6)] “Expression (7) implies that the effective sample is given by reweighting the original sample by the multiple regression weights—the $w_i$s. We may estimate each of the multiple regression weights with the estimator $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$.”

[Appendix A notation: p. 262 (PDF p. 13)] “Define $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$, a $K + 2$-length row vector combining the constant, causal factor, and control variables, and $\delta = (\alpha \quad \beta \quad \gamma)'$, a $K + 2$-length column vector containing the model coefficients. Define the stacked matrix of regressors and outcome vector as $\mathbf{W} = \begin{pmatrix} W_1 \\ \vdots \\ W_n \end{pmatrix}$ and $Y = \begin{pmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{pmatrix}$. The OLS estimates may be written as $\begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta \\ \hat\gamma_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat\gamma_k \end{pmatrix} = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$. By partial regression, $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$, (12) where $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$, with $\mathbf{V} = (V_1' \quad \cdots \quad V_n')'$, $D = (D_1 \quad \cdots \quad D_n)'$, and $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$.” (The last subscript of the coefficient column is printed $k$; the dimension is $K$: finding P015-N004.) Theorem A.1 writes the baseline outcome as $Y_{0i}$, the same object as $Y_i(0)$.

[General model of the section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: p. 260 (PDF p. 11)] “we now drop the assumption of local linearity, as stated by Expression (1). We instead define causal effects over arbitrary potential outcomes: $\tau_i(d, d') = \frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}$, where the $d$ and $d'$ in parentheses are to emphasize that causal effects are defined for treatment values $d$ and $d'$. … we continue to assume that $X_i$ is sufficient to control for all sources confounding between $D_i$ and outcomes that would be realized under treatments $d$ or $d'$. This is expressed formally as $(Y_i(d), Y_i(d')) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|X_i$. (11) Additionally, we no longer need to assume that the conditional expectation of $D_i$ is linear in the covariates.”

[Positivity: pp. 260–261 (PDF pp. 11–12)] “Positivity, loosely speaking, requires that, for all values of $X_i$ that appear in the target population, there is some probability of observing different values of $D_i$. … Formally, the positivity assumption is as follows: $\Pr[D_i = d|X_i = x] > 0, \quad \Pr[D_i = d'|X_i = x] > 0$ for all values of $x$ in the target population represented by the nominal sample. Given unconfoundedness and positivity, the average causal effect for the target population is defined by $\bar\tau(d, d') = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i(d, d')] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d')] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]}{d' - d}$. Expectations ($\mathrm{E}[.]$) are taken with respect to the target population.”

[Appendix C notation: p. 265 (PDF p. 16)] “$\Pr[Y_i = 1|D_i, X_i] = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_\ell + \beta_\ell D_i + X_i\gamma_\ell)$, where $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$. We fit the model via maximum likelihood (ML) to obtain the coefficient vector, $\hat\theta = (\hat\alpha_\ell \quad \hat\beta_\ell \quad \hat\gamma_\ell)'$. As before, let $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$. … $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$, where $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$”.

[Reading used by the targets; not printed] The units $(X_i, D_i, Y_i(\cdot))$ are treated as independent draws from one distribution (the super-population reading the paper allows on p. 252), and $\mathrm{E}[.]$, $\Pr[.]$, $\mathrm{Var}[.]$ refer to that distribution. The population form of the effective sample is the reweighted law $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w_i\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, defined when $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$; its mean of a covariate is $\mu(Z_i) = \mathrm{E}[w_iZ_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, as in Expression (9). Condition 4 of Theorem A.1 (“The data are well behaved such that the OLS solutions converge to a limit”) is read as the moment, law-of-large-numbers and nonsingularity conditions that the proof on pp. 262–263 uses (finding P015-A001, not confirmed as an error).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: ‘when a multiple regression places (either approximately or exactly) no weight on a set of units … positivity is violated and representative causal effects cannot be estimated …’, as printed (the ‘approximately’ case)
canonical_claim.location: p. 261 (PDF p. 12); positivity display on p. 261 (PDF p. 12); Expression (8) on p. 255 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed claim: p. 261 (PDF p. 12)] “The positivity assumption implies that $\mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i = x] > 0$, for all values of $x$. Thus, when a multiple regression places (either approximately or exactly) no weight on a set of units with a given covariate profile, this result implies that positivity is violated and representative causal effects cannot be estimated for the target population without assumption-based extrapolation or interpolation.” [Counterexample, from the validator] Fix $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$. Let $(X, D)$ take values in $\{0,1\}^2$ with $\Pr[X=0, D=0] = (1-\varepsilon)/2$, $\Pr[X=0, D=1] = \varepsilon/2$, $\Pr[X=1, D=0] = 1/4$, $\Pr[X=1, D=1] = 1/4$, and let the potential outcomes be $Y(d) = 2X + (1 + X)d$ for $d \in \{0, 1\}$. Then: (a) the paper’s assumptions hold: $Y(d) = Y(0) + \tau d$ with $Y(0) = 2X$ and $\tau = 1 + X$ (Expression (1)); $(Y(0), \tau)$ is a function of $X$, so $(Y(0), \tau) \perp\!\!\!\perp D | X$ (Expression (2)); $\mathrm{E}[D|X] = \varepsilon + (1/2 - \varepsilon)X$ (Expression (3)). (b) Positivity holds for $(d, d') = (0, 1)$: $\Pr[D=1|X=0] = \varepsilon$, $\Pr[D=0|X=0] = 1-\varepsilon$, $\Pr[D=1|X=1] = \Pr[D=0|X=1] = 1/2$, all $> 0$. (c) $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=0] = \varepsilon(1-\varepsilon) = 999999/10^{12}$ and $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=1] = 1/4$, so the effective-population mass of the profile $X = 0$ is $Q(X=0) = \frac{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon) + 1/4} = \frac{999999}{250000999999} < \frac{1}{250000}$, although its nominal mass is $1/2$. For every $0 < \varepsilon < 1/2$ the same construction has positivity and $0 < Q(X=0) < 4\varepsilon$, so no positive threshold for ‘approximately no weight’ implies a positivity violation. (d) A representative effect can be estimated without extrapolation: $\mathrm{E}[\tau] = 3/2$, and with $e(x) = \Pr[D=1|X=x]$ the inverse-probability-weighted variable $Z = \frac{DY}{e(X)} - \frac{(1-D)Y}{1-e(X)}$ (which uses only the observed $Y = Y(D)$) takes the values $0$, $10^6$, $-4$, $8$ on the four atoms in the order listed, with $\mathrm{E}[Z] = 3/2$, $\mathrm{E}[Z^2] = 500020$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Z) = 2000071/4$. Hence for independent draws $\bar Z_n = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i$ is unbiased for $\mathrm{E}[\tau]$ with variance $2000071/(4n)$, and $\Pr(|\bar Z_n - 3/2| \ge \delta) \le \frac{2000071}{4n\delta^2}$ for every $\delta > 0$ and $n \ge 1$, so $\bar Z_n$ is consistent. (e) The example agrees with Expression (7): the population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1, D, X)$ equals $\frac{\mathrm{E}[w\tau]}{\mathrm{E}[w]} = \frac{500000999999}{250000999999} \neq \frac{3}{2}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (Expression (8), p. 255, PDF p. 6); the effective sample as the reweighting of the sample by the $w_i$ and the estimated weights $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$ (p. 255, PDF p. 6); $\tau_i(d, d')$, unconfoundedness (11), the positivity display and $\bar\tau(d, d')$ (pp. 260–261, PDF pp. 11–12); all transcribed in the standing assumptions. Formal reading: ‘the weight a multiple regression places on the units with covariate profile $x$’ is the effective-population mass $Q(X = x) = \Pr[X = x]\,\mathrm{Var}[D|X = x]/\mathrm{E}[w]$, with $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w]$; in a sample it is the share $\sum_{i: X_i = x}\hat w_i/\sum_i \hat w_i$. ‘Positivity for $(d, d')$’ is the printed display at every $x$ with $\Pr[X = x] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: P015-E006 is rated an error, Moderate. The instance is the first validator's (derivation.md, section 2; exact checks in exact_checks.py and exact_output.txt). The second validator's instance (v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 3) uses $Y(t) = X + (1+X)t$ and gets $\mathrm{E}[Z^2] = 500010$, $\mathrm{Var}(Z) = 2000031/4$; either suffices. The Lean statement should be about this explicit four-point probability space: hypotheses (a)–(c) and the exact mean and variance of $Z$, with the Chebyshev bound for each $n$ as the finite form of consistency. Not claimed: good precision, or consistency uniform in $\varepsilon$. Not established by the validators: whether an extrapolation-free estimator exists for the actual Jensen target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: ‘the effective sample that multiple regression generates is one for which positivity holds by construction’, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 261 (PDF p. 12), right column; positivity display on p. 261 (PDF p. 12); $\tau_i(d, d')$ and (11) on p. 260 (PDF p. 11)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed claim: p. 261 (PDF p. 12)] “Of course, the effective sample that multiple regression generates is one for which positivity holds by construction.” The positivity it refers to is the display on the same page: “$\Pr[D_i = d|X_i = x] > 0, \quad \Pr[D_i = d'|X_i = x] > 0$ for all values of $x$ in the target population represented by the nominal sample.” [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $(X, D)$ be uniform on the four atoms $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,2)$ (probability $1/4$ each), so $D \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}[D|X] = 1/2 + X/2$, so Expression (3) holds. (b) The weights $w = (D - \mathrm{E}[D|X])^2$ on the four atoms are $1/4$, $1/4$, $1$, $1$: every unit has positive weight, $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=0] = 1/4$, $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=1] = 1$, and $\mathrm{E}[w] = 5/8$. (c) The effective law $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w]$ gives the atoms probabilities $1/10$, $1/10$, $2/5$, $2/5$, so $Q(X=0) = 1/5$ and $Q(X=1) = 4/5$: both covariate profiles are in the effective population. (d) $\Pr[D=1|X=1] = Q(D=1|X=1) = 0$, so the positivity display fails for $(d, d') = (0, 1)$ at $x = 1$, in the nominal and in the effective population. The conditional supports $\{0,1\}$ and $\{0,2\}$ meet only in $0$, so no pair $d \neq d'$ satisfies the display at both profiles. (e) The failure matters for identification under the section’s model (arbitrary potential outcomes with (11)): define two models with potential outcomes that are functions of $(X, d)$, $d \in \{0,1,2\}$. Model A: $Y(d) = d$. Model B: $Y(d) = d$ except that $Y(1) = 3$ when $X = 1$. In both, $(Y(0), Y(1), Y(2)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D | X$, and the observed outcome is $Y = D$ on every atom, so the joint laws of $(X, D, Y)$ coincide. But $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i(0,1)]$ is $1$ under A and $2$ under B, and under $Q$ it is $1$ under A and $13/5$ under B. Hence no function of the observed data is consistent for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i(0,1)]$ (nominal or effective) under both models.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (Expression (8), p. 255, PDF p. 6); the effective sample as the reweighting of the sample by the $w_i$ and the estimated weights $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$ (p. 255, PDF p. 6); $\tau_i(d, d')$, unconfoundedness (11), the positivity display and $\bar\tau(d, d')$ (pp. 260–261, PDF pp. 11–12); all transcribed in the standing assumptions. Formal reading: ‘the weight a multiple regression places on the units with covariate profile $x$’ is the effective-population mass $Q(X = x) = \Pr[X = x]\,\mathrm{Var}[D|X = x]/\mathrm{E}[w]$, with $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w]$; in a sample it is the share $\sum_{i: X_i = x}\hat w_i/\sum_i \hat w_i$. ‘Positivity for $(d, d')$’ is the printed display at every $x$ with $\Pr[X = x] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: From the first validator's derivation.md, section 3. The second validator's variant (v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 4) sets $Y(1) = 5$ at $X = 1$ and gets $1$ against $3$ (and $1$ against $21/5$ under $Q$). Model B violates Expression (1), which this section of the paper drops (p. 260: ‘we now drop the assumption of local linearity’); the example does not contradict Theorem A.1, and the population OLS coefficient is $1$ in both models. The sentence is true under the paper's loose gloss of positivity (‘some probability of observing different values of $D_i$’, p. 260) and for a binary treatment (P015-T4 (ii)–(iii)); it is false for the formal pair-specific display with a multivalued treatment, and both applications have multivalued treatments.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: ‘places (either approximately or exactly) no weight … this result implies that positivity is violated’, as printed (an exactly zero estimated weight in a sample)
canonical_claim.location: p. 261 (PDF p. 12); estimated weights $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$ on p. 255 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed claim: p. 261 (PDF p. 12)] “Thus, when a multiple regression places (either approximately or exactly) no weight on a set of units with a given covariate profile, this result implies that positivity is violated and representative causal effects cannot be estimated for the target population without assumption-based extrapolation or interpolation.” In an application the weights are the estimates of p. 255: “$\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$.” [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $X$ and $D$ be independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ variables. Positivity holds for $(0,1)$: $\Pr[D=d|X=x] = 1/2$ for all $d, x \in \{0,1\}$, and $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=x] = 1/4$ for both $x$. The ordered sample of size four $(X_i, D_i) = (0,0), (0,0), (1,0), (1,1)$ has probability $(1/4)^4 = 1/256 > 0$. In this sample the least-squares regression of $D$ on $V = (1 \quad X)$ has $\hat\omega = (0, 1/2)'$, residuals $\tilde D = (0, 0, -1/2, 1/2)$ and estimated weights $\hat w = (0, 0, 1/4, 1/4)$: every sampled unit with $X_i = 0$ has $\hat w_i = 0$ exactly. The regressors $(1, D, X)$ of Model (6) have Gram matrix $\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W} = \begin{pmatrix}4&1&2\\1&1&1\\2&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $2$, so the regression is defined. Hence an exactly zero estimated weight on a covariate profile implies neither $\mathrm{Var}[D|X=x] = 0$ nor a violation of positivity.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (Expression (8), p. 255, PDF p. 6); the effective sample as the reweighting of the sample by the $w_i$ and the estimated weights $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$ (p. 255, PDF p. 6); $\tau_i(d, d')$, unconfoundedness (11), the positivity display and $\bar\tau(d, d')$ (pp. 260–261, PDF pp. 11–12); all transcribed in the standing assumptions. Formal reading: ‘the weight a multiple regression places on the units with covariate profile $x$’ is the effective-population mass $Q(X = x) = \Pr[X = x]\,\mathrm{Var}[D|X = x]/\mathrm{E}[w]$, with $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w]$; in a sample it is the share $\sum_{i: X_i = x}\hat w_i/\sum_i \hat w_i$. ‘Positivity for $(d, d')$’ is the printed display at every $x$ with $\Pr[X = x] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: From the first validator's derivation.md, section 4, and the second validator's section 5 (same sample). It separates the fitted weights, which are what the paper reports for Jensen (2003), from the population weights: for population weights the exact-zero implication is true (P015-T4 (i)). The validators did not establish the population support of the Jensen data either way.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix C: the first-order Taylor expansion of $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}$ about $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)$, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 265 (PDF p. 16)] “We may approximate the $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(.)$ function by taking a first-order Taylor expansion about $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$, where $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$: $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) \approx P_Y + \frac{\exp[\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)]}{[1 + \mathrm{logit}(P_Y)]^2}[a - \mathrm{logit}(P_y)] = b + ca$, where $b = P_Y - P_Y(1 - P_Y)\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)$ and the scale factor $c = P_Y(1 - P_Y)$.” [Corrected display] $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) \approx P_Y + \frac{\exp[\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)]}{[1 + \exp[\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)]]^2}[a - \mathrm{logit}(P_Y)] = b + ca$, with $b$ and $c$ as printed. [Formal content] Let $f(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$ and $0 < P < 1$. (i) $f'(a) = \frac{\exp(a)}{[1 + \exp(a)]^2}$ for all real $a$. (ii) $f(\mathrm{logit}(P)) = P$ and $f'(\mathrm{logit}(P)) = \frac{\exp[\mathrm{logit}(P)]}{[1 + \exp[\mathrm{logit}(P)]]^2} = P(1 - P)$. (iii) Hence the first-order Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $\mathrm{logit}(P)$ is $P + P(1 - P)[a - \mathrm{logit}(P)] = b + ca$ with $b = P - P(1 - P)\mathrm{logit}(P)$ and $c = P(1 - P)$. (iv) The printed fraction $\frac{\exp[\mathrm{logit}(P)]}{[1 + \mathrm{logit}(P)]^2}$ is not this derivative: at $P = 1/2$ it equals $1$, while $f'(\mathrm{logit}(1/2)) = 1/4$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$, $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$ and $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$, with $0 < P_Y < 1$ (Appendix C, p. 265, PDF p. 16).
canonical_claim.note: P015-E010 is rated an error, Minor: $\exp$ is missing in the denominator of the displayed derivative, and the last bracket prints $P_y$ for $P_Y$. The constants $b$ and $c$ printed below the display are correct, and nothing depends on the misprint. The validator's check is in _batch/P015-B02/work/checks.py (output in checks-output.txt, verdict in _batch/P015-B02/verdicts.json). Part (iv) is the validator's instance against the printed fraction; it is kept inside this target because it is one evaluation.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 257: the Taylor approximation of the inverse logit for the weights, corrected (local first-order approximation)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected text, from Sol’s smallest repair] “A first-order Taylor expansion of the inverse link function provides a local approximation for the weights. Suppose we center this expansion on the logit of the mean of $Y_i$; its accuracy depends on how close the fitted linear predictors are to that center.” [Formal content, with every hypothesis] Let $f(a) = 1/(1 + e^{-a})$, $0 < P_Y < 1$ and $c_0 = \mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$. (i) The first-order Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $c_0$ is $T_1(a) = P_Y + P_Y(1 - P_Y)(a - c_0)$, and $f(a) - T_1(a) = O((a - c_0)^2)$ as $a \to c_0$. (ii) An increasing-order claim holds only on a restricted domain: the Taylor series of $f$ at the real center $c_0$ has radius of convergence $R(c_0) = \sqrt{c_0^2 + \pi^2}$ (the distance from $c_0$ to the nearest poles $\pm i\pi$ of $f$); if $0 \le r < \rho < R(c_0)$ and $M_\rho = \max_{|z - c_0| = \rho}|f(z)|$, then the Taylor polynomials $T_N$ of $f$ at $c_0$ satisfy $\sup_{|a - c_0| \le r}|f(a) - T_N(a)| \le M_\rho\frac{(r/\rho)^{N+1}}{1 - r/\rho} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. (iii) Outside that domain the claim fails: there are data with a unique finite maximum likelihood estimate whose fitted predictors lie outside the disk of convergence (P015-T11). No statement about the accuracy of the resulting coefficients or weights is asserted; that would need, in addition, a stability argument for the estimating equations.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = 1/[1 + \exp(-a)]$ (p. 257, PDF p. 8); $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$ and $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$ (Appendix C, p. 265, PDF p. 16). In (ii), $f$ is extended to complex $z$ by the same formula.
canonical_claim.note: From derivation.md, sections 3 and 6. Part (i) is the smallest repair and is the same first-order polynomial as $b + ca$ in Appendix C (P015-T13). Part (ii) is the validator's alternative repair, which keeps an increasing-order statement at the price of an explicit convergence-domain restriction (Cauchy's coefficient estimate); it is listed so that the formal content of both repairs is on record, and (i) alone satisfies the correction. The repair costs a weaker conclusion: the promise of arbitrary precision is withdrawn.
